title: CORS
subtitle: How Cross-Origin Resource Sharing works, preflight requests, and fixing CORS errors
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: A malicious website could use your logged-in credentials to make API requests on your behalf (CSRF). Without browser enforcement, a script on evil.com could call api.yourbank.com/transfer and your cookies would be sent automatically.
whyItExists.solution: The Same-Origin Policy blocks cross-origin requests by default. CORS is the opt-in mechanism that lets a server explicitly say 'I allow requests from other-origin.com'. The browser enforces this — server developers must configure it to allow trusted frontends.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any time your frontend (app.com) calls an API on a different origin (api.com or api.app.com). Both hosts, ports, and protocols must match for same-origin.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: CORS is a browser security mechanism. It doesn't affect server-to-server requests (Node.js backend calling another API) — only browser-to-server. Never use `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` for APIs that use cookies or Authorization headers.

explainModes.beginner: CORS is a browser safety rule. Your browser will refuse to let JavaScript on one website (like your app at localhost:3000) talk to a server at a different address (like api.example.com) UNLESS that server says 'yes, I allow requests from localhost:3000'. This is enforced by the browser — not the server. The error message 'CORS policy blocked' means the server hasn't allowed your origin. You fix it on the SERVER by adding Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers, not in your frontend code.
explainModes.simple: Same origin: same protocol + host + port. http://app.com:3000 ≠ https://app.com:3000 (different protocol). The server must respond with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://your-app.com. Simple requests: GET/POST with Content-Type text/plain, application/x-www-form-urlencoded, or multipart/form-data — no preflight. Preflighted requests: any other method or Content-Type (like JSON POST) triggers an OPTIONS preflight first. CORS never applies to server-side code — only browsers enforce it.
explainModes.standard: Preflight: browser sends OPTIONS request to ask 'can I send this?' before the actual request. Access-Control-Request-Method: POST. Access-Control-Request-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization. Server replies: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * or specific origin. Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE. Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization. Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400 (cache preflight for 24h). Credentials (cookies): fetch({credentials:'include'}) + server must respond Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true AND Access-Control-Allow-Origin must be a specific origin (not *).
explainModes.technical: CORS headers: request — Origin (browser sets, cannot be forged from JS). Response — Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers, Access-Control-Expose-Headers (which response headers JS can read), Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, Access-Control-Max-Age. Simple response headers readable by default: Cache-Control, Content-Language, Content-Length, Content-Type, Expires, Last-Modified, Pragma. All others need Access-Control-Expose-Headers. Express: `app.use(cors({ origin: 'https://app.com', credentials: true }))` from the cors npm package.
explainModes.deepDive: CORS bypass patterns: proxy server (frontend calls your-domain.com/proxy which forwards to third-party — same origin, no CORS check). JSONP (legacy hack for GET requests — loads script tag, third-party calls your callback). PostMessage (window.postMessage for iframe communication — separate CORS-bypass mechanism). Security auditing: check that your CORS config doesn't reflect arbitrary Origin header values — some buggy configs do `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: req.headers.origin` unconditionally, allowing any site to make credentialed requests. Vary: Origin header: CORS-enabling servers should include Vary: Origin in responses to prevent caches from serving the wrong CORS header to different origins.

content.text: CORS errors are a SERVER configuration problem, not a frontend problem. You cannot fix a CORS error by changing your fetch() call. The server needs to add Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers. During development, use your framework's dev proxy (Vite, webpack-dev-server, Next.js rewrites) to avoid CORS entirely.

questions.question: You get a CORS error: 'No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header present'. Where do you fix it?
options: Add a special header to your fetch() call in the frontend
On the server — add Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://your-app.com to the response headers. CORS is enforced by the browser based on headers the server sends back.
Set mode: 'no-cors' in your fetch() options
Use a newer browser that doesn't enforce CORS
questions.explanation: CORS is a browser security feature that checks response headers from the server. There is no frontend workaround — you must configure the server to include Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Note: fetch with `mode: 'no-cors'` creates an 'opaque' response — the request goes through but JavaScript gets back no data, headers, or status code. It's only useful for fire-and-forget requests (like sending analytics). For development, use a proxy in your build tool instead of dealing with CORS at all.

faq.q: Why does the CORS error say the request was blocked even though I can see it in the Network tab?
faq.a: CORS blocking is on the RESPONSE, not the request. The request reaches the server — you can see it in the Network tab, and the server processes it. The browser then checks the response headers. If Access-Control-Allow-Origin is missing or doesn't match, the browser blocks JavaScript from reading the response. This is why `mode: 'no-cors'` requests still reach the server but return no data to JavaScript — they're allowed to send but not to read the response.

usedIn: every frontend that calls a separate backend API
examples: Vite dev server proxy — avoids CORS in development by proxying /api to the backend
Stripe.js — stripe.com domain calls stripe.com API (same origin from their hosted checkout page)
GitHub API — Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * (wildcard, but no credentials needed)
